planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sweetheart is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though yields improve with a compatible sweet cherry nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting and avoid low, frost-prone planting sites. Sweetheart is a Canadian-bred sweet cherry from the Summerland research station in British Columbia, valued for being self-fertile — unlike Bing and many other sweet cherries, it sets a reliable crop without a separate pollinizer tree, making it a practical choice where space allows for only one cherry tree. It ripens notably late in the sweet cherry season, extending fresh harvest well after earlier cultivars like Bing and Rainier have finished, with medium-large, bright red, firm, sweet fruit of good flavor. The tree is vigorous and productive, and its self-fertility combined with late ripening has made it a popular choice for home orchards and small commercial plantings alike. Provide consistent moisture during fruit development to avoid cracking, especially if rain falls as fruit nears full ripeness.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center
Oregon State University Extension — Sweet Cherry Production
Summerland Research and Development Centre, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada

common_name: Carmine Jewel Cherry (Cold-Hardy Dwarf Bush Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Carmine Jewel is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator, and its compact, shrubby form fruits at a young age, often within 2-3 years of planting.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Carmine Jewel tolerates a wide range of soils and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Carmine Jewel is a University of Saskatchewan-bred dwarf sour cherry hybrid, part of a breeding program aimed at producing extremely cold-hardy, compact cherry shrubs for the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, where standard sweet and tart cherry trees cannot survive. The dense, shrubby plant stays under 8 feet tall, bears dark red, sweet-tart fruit good for fresh eating, baking, and preserves, and is self-fertile, bearing reliably without a second pollinator. Because of its extreme cold hardiness (surviving winter lows well below -40°F), it is grown mainly in northern climates outside the Gulf South's typical range, but is included here as a distinctive, easy-care option for gardeners in colder zones who want cherries without the size and chill-hour demands of standard cherry trees. Prune only lightly, removing dead or crossing wood, since the shrub form needs little training.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program — Carmine Jewel release notes
North Dakota State University Extension — Dwarf Sour Cherry Production

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Babcock has a low chill requirement (around 250-300 hours), making it well suited to mild-winter zones like the Gulf South where higher-chill peaches fail to fruit reliably.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Babcock is a heritage California peach dating to the late 1800s, valued for its low chill requirement and its white, sweet, low-acid, freestone flesh, quite different in character from the more common yellow-fleshed commercial peaches. The medium-sized fruit has a red-blushed, creamy-white skin and delicate, aromatic, honey-sweet flavor that is prized for fresh eating, though the tender white flesh bruises more easily than firmer yellow peaches and is less suited to shipping. Its low chill requirement makes it one of the more reliable white peaches for warm, mild-winter climates where standard high-chill peach varieties struggle to break dormancy properly. Thin fruit early to improve size and prevent limb breakage, and pick at full ripeness for the best flavor, since white peaches do not ripen further once picked.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Peach Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Peaches for Texas

common_name: Indian Free Peach (Red-Fleshed Heirloom Blood Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Indian Free is a late-ripening, low-chill heirloom peach with striking red-streaked flesh, valued as much for its unusual appearance and flavor as for fresh eating.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Indian Free is a distinctive American heirloom peach, likely of Native American cultivation origin, prized for its dramatic dark red, almost blood-colored flesh streaked through pale background flesh, and a rich, tangy-sweet, wine-like flavor unlike typical commercial peaches. It is a late-season variety, ripening well after most other peaches have finished, and shows notable resistance to peach leaf curl, a fungal disease that troubles many other peach cultivars in humid climates. The freestone fruit is best used fresh, in preserves, or in baking where its vivid color makes a striking presentation. Because it is an older, less commercially refined variety, fruit size and uniformity are more variable than modern hybrid peaches, but its unusual flavor and disease resistance have kept it popular among heirloom fruit collectors and home orchardists.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association — Peach Variety Notes
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom fruit archive
